answers.question: Is it feasible to accept a new order for 2,000 scarves due on May 15, 2026?
answers.answer:
Under the current capacity heuristic, accepting 2,000 scarves by May 15, 2026 is feasible only with workshops (FEASIBLE_WITH_WORKSHOPS).

The request was evaluated as ACCESSORIES. The model counts 39 working days and identifies PACKING as the bottleneck, with median throughput of 672 pieces per working day. Existing IN_PROGRESS orders account for 32,850 pieces, leaving estimated spare factory capacity at 0. Eligible ACTIVE workshops provide an estimated 12,831.05 pieces of overflow capacity, enough to cover the order.

This is a planning estimate, not a delivery guarantee. It treats every IN_PROGRESS order’s full quantity as competing demand because remaining quantities are unknown, uses the bottleneck median from the last 30 working days, does not model four-stage pipeline latency, assumes at most one new batch per workshop, and excludes SUSPENDED workshops.

answers.question: Explain the bottleneck and capacity assumptions in your feasibility result.
answers.answer:
The feasibility result used these assumptions:

Factory bottleneck

• PACKING was the bottleneck because it had the lowest 30-working-day median throughput: 672 pieces per working day.
• The window from April 1 through May 15 contains 39 working days, counting Monday–Saturday and excluding Sundays.
• The model therefore set factory window capacity at 26,208 pieces.
• It treated all 32,850 pieces on IN_PROGRESS orders as competing workload. Because that exceeds the modeled window capacity, spare in-house capacity was clipped to 0.

This is conservative because the dataset does not show how many pieces remain unfinished on each active order; it assumes each order’s entire quantity is still outstanding.

Workshop capacity

Only ACTIVE workshops that make ACCESSORIES were included: W2, W4, and W6. For each workshop:

• Available production days = working days minus pickup lead time and existing queue.
• Output = daily capacity × available days × (1 − defect rate).
• Any maximum batch limit would cap that output.
• The model assumes no more than one new batch per workshop during the window.

Their combined estimated overflow capacity was 12,831.05 pieces. Since the factory had 0 modeled spare capacity but workshop capacity could cover the requested 2,000 scarves, the verdict was FEASIBLE_WITH_WORKSHOPS.

The estimate does not model the timing needed to move work sequentially through knitting, assembly, washing, and packing, so it is a capacity check—not a delivery guarantee.

   It has the shortest estimate in the second-priority bucket at 2.0 working days. Keep ORD-029, ORD-083, and ORD-002 moving as the rest of the second-priority Washing group; ORD-029 is due today.
3. In Assembly, work ORD-120 before ORD-108 and ORD-103.
   ORD-120 is in the second-priority overdue group. ORD-108 and ORD-103 are third priority but likely to miss their upcoming dates at the current pace.
4. Give Assembly management attention today.
   It is the only stage running materially below its normal output, so resolving that slowdown is important to prevent additional late orders.

This schedule follows the official priority buckets; only the choice of ORD-093 within the tied second-priority group is an operational tie-break based on shortest estimated remaining work.

answers.question: Why is ORD-107 at risk?
answers.answer:
ORD-107 is not merely at risk—it is already overdue. It was due 2026-03-16, remains in Packing, and has 3.0 estimated working days left.

That 3.0-day figure is calculated as:

max(sum of pieces ÷ 30-day median output for each remaining stage, number of remaining stages)

Because Packing is its only remaining stage, the estimate uses the packing pace for its 2,000 pieces, with a minimum of one day. It is therefore 1st priority: overdue but close to completion.
